name: PL/SQL
title: PL/SQL (Oracle 26ai)
lifecycleNote: Oracle AI Database 26ai, the long-term-support release that replaces 23ai; on-premises general availability followed in January 2026.

type.text: **Static typing over SQL data types**: Every variable, constant, parameter, and function return declares a type, and a mismatch is a compilation error
**`%TYPE` and `%ROWTYPE` anchor a declaration to the schema**: `emp%ROWTYPE` follows the table's column list, so a column change does not require editing the declaration
**Subtypes declare a constrained domain once**: `SUBTYPE` and a constrained type such as `NUMBER(7,2)` state a range or a shape and reuse it
**NULL is not type-safe absence (T10)**: An unassigned variable and an unused column are NULL, and NULL propagates through expressions, so `IF x = 5` is not true when `x` is NULL
**A `REF CURSOR` carries a row set without fixing its row type**: `SYS_REFCURSOR` passes a result between program units, so the producer and the consumer need not share a record type

construction.text: **The package separates specification from body**: The spec declares the public interface — types, variables, constants, exceptions, cursors, and subprograms — and the body holds the implementation, so a consumer binds to the spec
**Subprogram overloading is available in a package**: Two subprograms with one name differ by parameter list, so a family of operations shares one name
**A cursor `FOR ... LOOP` iterates the query result directly**: Iteration ends at the result's last row, so the code does not track a row count
**Global mutable state by default (C1)**: A package variable is declared once and lives for the whole session, so every caller that touches the package sees and changes the same value
**Package initialisation runs on first use**: An initialisation block in the body runs when the package is first touched in the session, so setup timing follows call order
**Triggers fire implicitly**: A trigger runs in response to an insert, update, or delete, so the writer of a statement cannot see from the statement which code will run

memory.text: **No manual memory management**: The Oracle server owns SGA and PGA memory, and a block never names an address or frees a byte
**The server sizes the work areas**: Automatic PGA management gives a sort or a hash operation its memory from `PGA_AGGREGATE_TARGET`, so the block does not reserve it
**A session-scoped collection holds its memory**: An associative array or nested table kept in a package variable stays for the session, so retained state is a standing cost
**A bulk fetch needs a deliberate size limit**: `BULK COLLECT ... LIMIT` bounds a fetch, and its absence can materialise a whole result set in PGA
**A cursor is released by `CLOSE`**: The server reclaims the cursor's memory, so the program does not track bytes

error.text: **The block separates the normal path from the recovery path**: `DECLARE ... BEGIN ... EXCEPTION ... END;` gives a named handler section

**Exceptions are matched by name**: A predefined exception (`NO_DATA_FOUND`, `TOO_MANY_ROWS`, `ZERO_DIVIDE`) and a user-declared `EXCEPTION` are caught by name, and `WHEN OTHERS` catches the remainder
**`RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR` sets a code and a message**: A custom failure carries a number in the application range −20000 to −20999, so a caller can branch on it

**`WHEN OTHERS` hides the class of the failure (Er3)**: A handler that catches everything without logging `SQLCODE` and `SQLERRM`, or that does not re-raise, lets the enclosing block see a normal return where the inner block failed
**No composable result type (Er4)**: A failure cannot be returned as a value the caller must inspect, so error information does not compose through a call chain

concurrency.text: **Transactions are the unit of concurrency**: `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, and `SAVEPOINT` make a unit of work atomic, so a block does not coordinate with other sessions statement by statement
**An autonomous transaction decouples a log write**: `PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION` commits on its own, so the entry survives the caller's rollback
**`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` names the rows to lock**: The lock is declared by the cursor text rather than by a separate call
**Shared mutable state by default (K2)**: A package variable is shared with every program unit that runs in the session, and nothing in the declaration marks it private

**Serialisation across sessions is the application's to arrange**: Where row locks do not apply, two sessions coordinate only through an explicit `DBMS_LOCK` call, and the ordering between them is nowhere declared
**`DBMS_LOCK` provides an explicit lock service**: A named user lock serialises a critical section across sessions

platform.text: **The block and package model follows the SQL/PSM shape**: Persistent stored modules are specified in ISO/IEC 9075 Part 4, and the package and block model follows that concept, though the language itself has no public specification
**It is implemented outside Oracle Database**: TimesTen and IBM Db2 support PL/SQL, so there is more than one implementation, though the dialects are not fully interchangeable
**Cannot function outside one vendor (P1)**: A PL/SQL program needs an Oracle-family database, so the unit of deployment is an Oracle schema
**The useful surface is Oracle-specific**: `DBMS_*` server packages, `ROWNUM`, sequences, and `SQL%ROWCOUNT` are Oracle features, so the code cannot move to another engine unedited
**A port to Transact-SQL is a rewrite, not a translation**: Feature differences and different concurrency and locking models separate the two dialects

performance.text: **Compilation happens at deployment**: A package or procedure is compiled once and the stored form is reused, so a call does not re-parse the source
**Native compilation is selectable**: `PLSQL_CODE_TYPE = NATIVE` compiles to machine code, so a hot subprogram does not pay the interpreter
**Bulk processing amortises the SQL boundary**: `FORALL` and `BULK COLLECT` move many rows per round trip, so per-row context switches do not dominate
**The optimiser and the SGA serve the data path**: Plan selection and buffer caching are the server's job, not the block's
**Cost follows the plan and the retained state**: A poorly chosen plan, or a package variable holding a large collection, is a cost the unit cannot see

ecosystem.text: **The ecosystem is proprietary (Ec4)**: The engine, the tooling, and the support come from Oracle under licence
**Tooling is mature and long-established**: SQL\*Plus, SQL Developer, and third-party IDEs have existed for decades
**Published practice is extensive**: The PL/SQL language reference, the database manuals, and decades of books and courses document the language in detail
**Capability follows the licence**: Tooling, support, and advanced features are licensed per seat or per processor, so a team reaches only what it has bought
**Enterprise code bases are long-lived and heavy**: A schema commonly spans many versions, so a change has to keep the oldest callers working

evolution.text: **Backward compatibility is strong**: A program written for an early Oracle release generally still compiles and runs in the current one
**Edition-based redefinition supports an online change**: `EDITIONABLE` objects let a new version of a package be deployed and switched over without downtime
**Deprecation is announced before removal**: Oracle documents deprecated features, so an upgrade is planned rather than discovered
**A language feature arrives with a database release**: Adoption timing therefore follows the customer's upgrade cycle, not a separate language release
**A new feature is unavailable on a pinned older database**: Code that must run on an old release cannot use a recent construct

domain.text: **Excellent fit for data-centric business logic**: A procedure operates on tables with SQL directly, so a rule runs where the data is
**The language is a full procedural language inside SQL**: Loops, records, collections, and subprograms live in the same unit as the queries
**Server packages reach outside the schema**: `UTL_FILE`, `UTL_HTTP`, and `DBMS_SCHEDULER` give file, network, and job facilities from inside the database
**Domain and vendor lock-in (D1)**: The language exists to run inside an Oracle database, so the Oracle data tier is the only domain
**A trigger can hide a domain rule**: An invariant implemented in a trigger is enforced for every writer, but a reader of the application source cannot see it
**The language is not a general-purpose runtime**: A user interface, a heavy text workload, or a high-rate service belongs in another language beside PL/SQL

learning.text: **Moderate for a SQL-plus-Pascal background**: The block structure follows Ada and Pascal, so a developer from those languages reads it quickly
**The SQL-to-PL/SQL boundary needs practice**: A `SELECT` inside a block must return exactly one row, so `NO_DATA_FOUND` and `TOO_MANY_ROWS` are everyday cases
**Package semantics take time**: Spec versus body, per-session package state, and initialisation timing are not visible in the syntax
**Exception semantics reward careful reading**: An exception in a nested block propagates to the enclosing handler unless it is handled there
**The reference documentation is complete**: The Oracle Database PL/SQL Language Reference documents every construct with examples

syntax.text: **Readable and keyword-led**: Statements read as verbs — `INSERT INTO`, `FETCH`, `RAISE` — so intent is visible
**Blocks nest visibly**: An inner `BEGIN ... END` holds its own declarations and handler, so scope follows the indentation
**Verbose (S1)**: Even a small unit needs a declaration section, a `BEGIN ... END`, and an exception section, so the block structure adds lines to every subprogram
**`END` closes several constructs**: `END IF;`, `END LOOP;`, and a package `END` must each be matched, so a long body is read against its terminators
**A large package body is one long file**: The spec and the body are a unit boundary, not a file-per-subprogram rule

testing.text: **`utPLSQL` is the established framework**: An open-source test framework runs suites with assertions and reporting, so tests need not be hand-rolled
**Transaction control isolates a test**: A test can run and `ROLLBACK`, leaving the database unchanged
**The toolchain traces execution**: `DBMS_PROFILER`, `DBMS_TRACE`, and the hierarchical profiler report call counts and coverage
**A suite depends on grants and deployment**: The framework is installed in the database it tests, so permissions and schema state are preconditions

security.text: **Bind variables remove the injection surface**: `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE 'SELECT ... WHERE x = :1' USING v` passes the value out of band, so it cannot change the parse
**`DBMS_ASSERT` validates an identifier before interpolation**: `SIMPLE_SQL_NAME`, `QUALIFIED_SQL_NAME`, and `ENQUOTE_NAME` check the string
**The rights model is explicit**: `AUTHID DEFINER` and `AUTHID CURRENT_USER` select whether a unit runs with its owner's privileges or the caller's
**Privileges are granted per object**: `GRANT EXECUTE ON pkg TO role` scopes access, and the package specification is the grantable interface
**Known vulnerability/injection (Q3)**: `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` and `DBMS_SQL` build a statement as text, so concatenated input can become code
**Definer's-rights code can escalate**: A unit that runs with its definer's rights reaches more than the caller, so it needs an audit

tradeoffs: **A session-scoped package variable is a deliberate cache**: Keeping a value for the session avoids a repeated read; the cost is staleness, since nothing invalidates the cached value when the underlying data changes
**A trigger is a data-integrity mechanism**: A rule kept in the database is enforced for every writer, where the same rule in the application would be visible at each call site

**Logic beside the data is the purpose of the language**: A procedure that runs in the database avoids shipping rows to a client; the cost is that the rule sits outside the application's test suite and profilers
**Dynamic SQL buys flexibility**: `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` runs DDL and changes object names in a statement, which static SQL cannot do; the cost is that the statement's shape is known only when it runs
verdict: PL/SQL's coupling is set by its host, not its syntax. The package separates a specification from its body, blocks and named exceptions give a structured failure path, and bind variables close the injection surface. Main strengths: interface and implementation are separable, error handling is structured, and server-side code runs beside its data. Main weaknesses: everything runs inside an Oracle database, a package variable is shared session state, every variable starts as NULL and NULL propagates, dynamic SQL turns concatenated text into code, and `WHEN OTHERS` is a standing invitation to swallow a failure.

energy.text: Runs inside a database engine: energy and time are the engine's, not the program's.

ai-readiness.text: Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [@joel2025lowresource].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

delivery.note: The database stores the source text and parses it; no compiled unit crosses a boundary
